title: Create a project virtual environment (reference)
description:
Source item 1: create a project directory with a virtual environment.

This is a shell/tooling task, not Python code - there is nothing here for a hidden test to check. The steps: `mkdir my_project && cd my_project`, `python -m venv venv` (creates an isolated `venv/` folder with its own Python and package set), then activate it - `source venv/bin/activate` on macOS/Linux, `venv\Scripts\activate` on Windows. Your shell prompt changes to show the active environment; `pip install <package>` from that point installs only into `venv/`, not system-wide. `deactivate` leaves the environment.
examples:
$ mkdir my_project && cd my_project
$ python -m venv venv
$ source venv/bin/activate
(venv) $ pip install requests
(venv) $ deactivate
$

hints: This entry documents the real workflow rather than asking you to write code - there's no fixed output for a virtual environment to print.
python -m venv <name> is the standard-library way to create one - no separate package (like virtualenv) is required on a modern Python install.
Try it directly in a terminal: create one, activate it, run `pip list` to see it starts nearly empty, then deactivate and run `pip list` again to see the difference.

explanation: A virtual environment is just a self-contained copy of the Python interpreter plus an empty (or nearly empty) site-packages directory - activating it changes which `python`/`pip` your shell finds first, so installs go there instead of system-wide.
